Everything This Page Would Like To Run

Stored content is sanitized once, on the way into the database, and every consumer afterwards reads it without a sanitizer of its own. That is a good arrangement and it is also a single point of failure, so the thing it protects against belongs in a fixture that actually attempts it rather than in a comment asserting that it would be caught.

A paragraph whose click handler is an attempt to run code the moment the reader touches the text. The paragraph itself is ordinary prose and should be kept; only the handler has to go, which is what makes this harder than dropping the element.

An image whose error handler is the payload, because an address that cannot load is the most reliable way to be called:

A link whose target is a script rather than a page. The text is worth keeping and the target is not, so the attribute goes and the sentence stays readable.

A frame pointing somewhere else, which in a reader would be another origin's page rendered inside this one:

Two older ways of asking for a plugin, both of which still parse:

A style attribute carrying a url(), which is a request to a third party made by the act of rendering the article, and a position that would lift an element out of the page and over whatever is behind it:

Text under a style attribute that asks for two things it should not get and one, a colour, that it may keep.

Form controls, because a page that can render a password field inside a trusted reader can ask for a password that looks like it belongs there:

Why the prose matters

None of the above is unusual on its own; a real page carries analytics, an embedded video and a newsletter form without meaning anyone harm. The sanitizer cannot tell intent apart from accident and should not try, so it keeps the small set of elements an article is made of and drops everything else, including the things that were only ever decoration.

The cost is that a legitimately embedded video does not survive either. That is the right trade for a reader whose whole job is to show someone else's text, and the snapshot is kept precisely so the original page is still there when the embedded thing was the point.
